passages.title: Role of the volunteers
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Role of the volunteers"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a representative of Elmley Town Council speaking to people who are interested in joining the Small Towns Volunteer Scheme. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Good morning everyone.

[00:52] AUDIO: I'm Steve Wainwright from Elmley Town Council and I coordinate the town's volunteer scheme. It's great to see that so many of you are thinking of taking part. The scheme helps strengthen connections among people in our historic town of Elmley. Our volunteers also make both local residents and visitors feel at home during community events.

[01:18] AUDIO: Let me begin by describing some of the jobs they do. One duty involves walking through the streets in the town centre in an official volunteer t-shirt. Visitors regularly stop our team to ask for directions to shops or for suggestions about places worth seeing. Elmley stages many concerts during the year.

[01:43] AUDIO: At these events volunteers guide members of the audience to the correct section so that people can settle down without delays. Quite a few ticket holders fail to read their tickets properly and make for the wrong part of the hall. Volunteers can also support local organisations including sports clubs and gardening societies. Their task there is to show different groups how they might work together.

[02:15] AUDIO: For example, a writing club may be planning a trip to hear a famous author in another town without realising that a different association has a coach available. We publish a magazine every month and any resident may contribute an article. Local companies fund it, but approaching those businesses is handled by the Council's advertising team. What we ask volunteers to do is speak to people who have attended town events, gather their reactions and future suggestions and send a brief report to the editors.

[02:56] AUDIO: We also arrange a yearly lunch for members of the town's clubs for retired residents. Volunteers greet everyone on arrival. Once the meal is over and the guests are comfortable, several volunteers perform about thirty minutes of songs and short sketches. The guests also enjoy having time to talk with the team.

[03:23] AUDIO: Naturally the Council has its own website. Volunteers help spread the word about it among local people. New details about upcoming activities are added daily and we'd like far more residents to check it regularly. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.

[04:20] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Now that you have an idea of the work involved, I'll cover a few practical points. Elmley runs three large festivals each year and each one relies on a substantial volunteer team. The book festival runs for three days across several locations, all of which need helpers.

[04:47] AUDIO: The music festival lasts an entire week so it calls for a bigger team. The science festival needs the most assistance of all despite lasting only two days because activities are spread across so many venues. Choosing a festival that genuinely interests you is sensible as volunteers can attend most sessions without paying. Adaptability is useful too some activities take place outside and the weather can alter audience numbers or even cause a cancellation, sometimes with very little warning.

[05:28] AUDIO: The quality we consider absolutely necessary however is the ability to relate well to other people. That includes dealing calmly with anyone whose behavior becomes difficult, which does happen from time to time. We intend to have all of you begin your duties in September. Training starts in the week beginning the second and continues for one week so your first shifts will be scheduled from the ninth.

[06:02] AUDIO: During the week beginning the 23rd we'll meet each of you to discuss how you're finding the role and whether you need any additional support. Each year we hold a special event to thank our volunteers. A few years ago it was a party at the Town Hall while last year's event was a barbecue in Chamber Park. This time we've arranged a boat journey along the canal from Elmley to Dewhurst and back.

[06:34] AUDIO: It takes place on Saturday September 28th and you'll be able to register once your volunteering begins. Right, let me show you the volunteer t-shirt now. That is the end of part two. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Human geography
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Human geography"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students, Rosie and Colin, talking about an assignment for their Human Geography course. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
[00:49] ROSIE: Colin, I can't seem to settle on a subject for our Human Geography assignment.
[00:54] COLIN: I'm having the same problem. Why don't we go through the different areas of the subject? That might help us reduce the options and choose one.
[01:03] ROSIE: Alright. Population is one possibility. We'd cover things such as where people are concentrated and how they move between places. There'd be a lot of numerical information.
[01:14] ROSIE: It doesn't sound especially exciting though.
[01:17] COLIN: True, but we shouldn't have any trouble getting the material online.

[01:21] ROSIE: I suppose not. What about health? I hadn't realized geography was connected with it until Professor Lee's session on cholera. She explained how a 19th century doctor compared street maps with diagrams of the water network to trace an outbreak back to its source.
[01:41] COLIN: I found that really absorbing too. Another option would be a broader topic such as economics.
[01:48] ROSIE: You mean the relationship between finance, business, and the physical surroundings?
[01:53] COLIN: Exactly.
[01:54] ROSIE: I thought it had been removed from this year's course program.
[01:58] COLIN: Really?
[01:59] ROSIE: I'm not completely certain, but perhaps we shouldn't choose it.
[02:03] COLIN: Fair enough. Culture's another possibility. We had a class on cultural geography last week.
[02:10] ROSIE: It wasn't much help to me. Everything stayed at such a broad level and the lecturer didn't use any concrete examples.
[02:17] COLIN: Same here. I hardly wrote anything down because there didn't seem much point.
[02:23] ROSIE: Nor did I.
[02:24] COLIN: We might concentrate on poverty. It's an issue affecting the whole world.
[02:30] ROSIE: The difficulty, as Dr. Lee pointed out, is that some poverty statistics need to be treated cautiously. At times, the figures are altered on purpose.
[02:41] COLIN: For political motives, you mean?
[02:43] ROSIE: Yes, things like that.
[02:46] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

[03:31] ROSIE: So, which topic shall we actually use for the assignment? Wait, there's one area we haven't considered. Urbanization. More than half of the world's population now live in cities, so it's a major issue.
[03:44] COLIN: That works for me. Good suggestion, Rosie. Let's choose that.
[03:49] ROSIE: I enjoy living in a large city, although there are obviously difficulties.
[03:55] COLIN: You mean things like burglary and street crime?

[03:58] ROSIE: Yes, but in my city that's connected with a more serious concern. There simply aren't enough employment opportunities. And the situation is continuing to deteriorate. We still have plenty of people without somewhere to live as well, although that problem has eased a little.
[04:16] COLIN: We should include some encouraging changes too, perhaps the new facilities being built beyond city centers.
[04:23] ROSIE: Yes. Several enormous retail complexes have opened outside my city.

[04:28] COLIN: Mine too, though they've caused many central shops to go out of business. The edge of a city is useful for buildings that require a great deal of land, such as large conference venues. Two have opened near me.
[04:42] ROSIE: We've got some of those as well, and they've been a real improvement. I'd also welcome more places for sports like football, but none are being added where I live.
[04:52] COLIN: It's the same in my area.
[04:55] ROSIE: What about mentioning the redevelopment of abandoned industrial land? It seems sensible because it avoids disturbing untouched, natural areas.
[05:05] COLIN: But couldn't the old buildings have architectural value?

[05:08] ROSIE: Most of them don't. A bigger concern is that factories often left hazardous substances behind, and these may never have been removed properly. The land then has to be cleaned up before anyone can use it.
[05:23] COLIN: That must cost a fortune. And developers probably don't always allow for it in their original budgets.
[05:30] ROSIE: Exactly.
[05:31] COLIN: Have you come across Masdar City?

[05:34] ROSIE: The project in Abu Dhabi? Yes. It was planned as an environmentally responsible city, wasn't it? It would be a useful example of a place intended to operate entirely on renewable power.
[05:47] COLIN: Agreed. We should include that. The original plan also kept cars off the streets with transport running below ground.
[05:56] ROSIE: Yes, and there were ambitious recycling proposals designed to minimize waste. But for our assignment, let's limit the Masdar example to its energy supply.

[06:08] COLIN: Then there's Greenhill Abbots, the proposed ecotown in England. Its aims followed the usual ideas about sustainability. It attracted a lot of criticism at the beginning because people thought the plans couldn't be achieved. What I don't know is how much of the development has actually been completed.
[06:28] COLIN: I'll find out.
[06:29] ROSIE: Good. It sounds as though we've got the basis of our plan now.
[06:36] NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 3. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

passages.title: Developing food trends
content: 📌 Developing food trends
• Interest in new food fashions increased after [ _____ ] showing meals began to circulate online.
• The UK food sector continually searches for unfamiliar or distinctive products.
• Social-media personalities act as brand ambassadors.
• Companies offering [ _____ ] products were early users of this method and saw sales rise quickly.
• Supermarkets analyse online interest in products and ingredients.
• Their choices are strongly influenced by what celebrated [ _____ ] put on their menus.

Marketing campaigns
The avocado
A group of [ _____ ] travelled to South Africa at the agency's expense to meet avocado growers.Advertisements emphasised the fruit's benefits for [ _____ ].
Oat milk
In the USA, supplying [ _____ ] chains meant that a large advertising budget was unnecessary.The product appealed to buyers who wanted to cause less harm to the [ _____ ].
Norwegian skrei
The campaign enhanced the [ _____ ] of seafood produced in Norway.
Ethical concerns: quinoa
As demand peaked, its [ _____ ] rose so sharply that local residents could not afford it.Continuous cultivation caused a serious decline in the fertility of the [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a food science lecture about changing fashions in food. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Food goes in and out of fashion in much the same way as clothes do.

[00:53] AUDIO: Public enthusiasm for new food trends began rising quickly with the arrival of smartphones. That was when people started photographing their meals and immediately sending the images to friends online. The food business in the UK is especially keen to identify the next major craze and make the most of it. Marketing teams try to generate enormous demand for an item that consumers may not previously have known about or even felt they needed.

[01:27] AUDIO: One particularly powerful method is to turn social media influences into ambassadors for a brand. Many will publish posts in exchange for complementary products while those with audiences numbering in the hundreds of thousands may charge substantial fees. Firms producing vegan goods were among the first to show just how rapidly this approach could drive up sales. Of course, no food can become widely popular unless people can buy it easily, so supermarkets also help shape new trends.

[02:05] AUDIO: Their specialist teams monitor which products and ingredients are gaining attention online. They pay especially close attention to the dishes that famous chefs are adding to their menus. Let me now consider several campaigns that were extremely effective in turning particular foods into major trends. I'll begin with the avocado in the 1990s.

[02:32] AUDIO: A public relations agency in Britain was employed to make the fruit better known and increase demand. The agency paid for a group of journalists to visit South Africa and meet avocado growers. The reports produced after the trip taught British consumers more about the fruit, which was far from being an everyday food at that point. The advertisements presented avocado as a nutrient-rich superfood and stressed its benefits for health.

[03:04] AUDIO: The fruit soon became highly fashionable. Within a few years, annual UK sales rose from £13 million to roughly £150 million, making this one of the country's most successful campaigns for fresh produce. Oat milk provides a more recent example of a product that became fashionable in a very short time. Although many versions are sold now, the Swedish company Oatly was one of the brands that succeeded early.

[03:37] AUDIO: It drew widespread notice by deliberately using provocation in its media campaign. Irritating producers of dairy milk was actually helpful because the controversy gave oat milk a fashionable image. In the United States, the company chose not to begin with a large retail launch. Instead, it supplied coffee chains, which meant it did not need a huge advertising budget.

[04:05] AUDIO: This worked much better than handing out samples in supermarkets. Oat milk also had an edge over other substitutes such as almond milk. Many customers chose it because it caused less damage to the environment. It takes considerably less water to make and has a comparatively small carbon footprint.

[04:27] AUDIO: Another case is Norwegian Scray, a seasonal delicacy also called Arctic Cod, and available for only a limited period. It now appears on menus in Michelin-starred restaurants across Europe. A food marketing organisation has used demand for Scree to improve the reputation of Norway's fisheries more generally. Consumer research indicates that many shoppers now connect Norway with seafood of excellent quality.

[05:00] AUDIO: In certain respects, food fashions can be beneficial, particularly because farmers and other producers may gain considerably. They can also persuade the public to purchase foods made in more sustainable ways. However, a sudden rise in demand can also create ethical problems. Quinoa is a well-known example.

[05:26] AUDIO: The crop originated in Peru, and when demand reached its height several years ago, its price shot up. Local people could no longer afford to buy it. Quinoa's popularity did improve farmers' incomes, but it brought harmful effects as well. To increase output, farmers began planting the crop throughout the year.

[05:50] AUDIO: As a result, the fertility of the soil fell dramatically. And in some places, this may eventually cause desertification. A further example would be the case of... That is the end of part four.

[06:08] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four. That is the end of the listening test. In the IELTS test, you would now have ten minutes to transfer your answers to the listening answer sheet.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a woman calling the owner of a house she is about to rent to ask about local furniture rental companies. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.
[00:49] LANDLORD: Good morning.
[00:50] SHELLEY: Hello, it's Shelley Meyer. I'm renting your property on Archwood Avenue, and I'm moving in next week.
[00:57] LANDLORD: Oh yes, Miss Meyer, how can I help?

[01:00] SHELLEY: When I came to see the house, I mentioned that I'd probably have to hire some furniture. My work contract is temporary for now, so I don't want to buy everything until I know whether the job will become permanent.
[01:14] LANDLORD: Yes, I remember. I said I could tell you about a few furniture hire companies in the city.
[01:20] SHELLEY: Exactly.
[01:21] LANDLORD: The largest one is Peak Rentals. I've sent several tenants to them, and the comments I've heard have always been favorable.
[01:29] SHELLEY: Can you give me a rough idea of what they charge?
[01:32] LANDLORD: I've got their leaflet here. The monthly rate for furnishing one room begins at $105 and can be as high as $239, depending on which rooms you want equipped.
[01:45] SHELLEY: That's fine. I just need an approximate figure for my budget. And what did people particularly like about Peak Rentals?

[01:52] LANDLORD: They said Peak's furniture was more modern than the pieces supplied by any of the other firms. Delivery is quick, too. Once the order has been confirmed, it normally arrives within one or two days.
[02:06] SHELLEY: That speed would certainly help.
[02:08] LANDLORD: There's also a promotion running now. If you hire a living room set, that means the chairs and a table for the television. They include a lamp free of charge.
[02:19] SHELLEY: That sounds useful, but the overall price range is higher than I'd hoped.
[02:24] LANDLORD: In that case, you could look at Aaron and Oliver.
[02:27] SHELLEY: Sorry, what was the first name?
[02:29] LANDLORD: Aaron. It's spelt A-A-R-O-N.
[02:35] SHELLEY: Right. Are their rates lower?
[02:37] LANDLORD: I'd describe them as mid-range. However, they add 12% to the monthly bill to cover possible damage. So remember to include that when you calculate the cost.
[02:49] SHELLEY: I see. I'll need to work that out carefully.
[02:53] LANDLORD: They can also provide a cleaning service for clients.
[02:56] SHELLEY: Do you mean cleaning the furniture?
[02:58] LANDLORD: No, the house itself.
[03:00] SHELLEY: Oh, right. I doubt I'll require that.
[03:06] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
[03:47] LANDLORD: Another option is large furniture. It is only recently opened, and its prices are the lowest in the city. That applies both to furniture and to electronic equipment.
[04:00] SHELLEY: That could suit me. I'm bringing very little, and once I start work, I won't have much time to shop.
[04:07] LANDLORD: There are two conditions you should know about. First, the furniture has to be insured, and you must arrange the insurance yourself.
[04:16] SHELLEY: That shouldn't be difficult.
[04:18] LANDLORD: Second, there are contracts run for at least six months. I don't imagine that will cause you a problem since your agreement for the house is for 12 months.
[04:27] SHELLEY: No, that should be fine.
[04:29] LANDLORD: Sorry to cut in, but I've just remembered one more business. It's called Space Rentals, and it's very close to the house.
[04:37] SHELLEY: Okay.
[04:38] LANDLORD: I don't have their current rates, so the best way to check the latest prices is through their app.
[04:43] SHELLEY: Thanks. I'll have a look.
[04:45] LANDLORD: One advantage is that if the furniture isn't right once it arrives, exchanges are allowed. You just need to ask within seven days of delivery.
[04:54] SHELLEY: That's excellent. Thanks very much. This has been really helpful.
[05:01] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Community project
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Community project"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear an archaeologist involved in a community excavation, explaining the site to a group of visitors. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now, listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Hello, I'm Hayden, one of the archaeologists working here at Bidcaster.

[00:55] AUDIO: This is the project's third summer, and nearly everyone carrying out the excavation is a volunteer. My permanent post is with the town council, but it was NHA that invited me to take part. It's a charity that organises projects of this kind throughout the country. Being beside Bidcaster Castle is useful too, since the castle's owners allow us to use their facilities.

[01:22] AUDIO: You may be wondering how the work began. Archaeological investigations often start after someone comes across an old object, and here the first discovery was a gold coin. People sometimes locate coins with metal-detecting equipment, while rabbits and other animals can expose them by disturbing the ground. Neither happened here.

[01:45] AUDIO: A walker noticed this one lying on the surface after a heavy downpour had carried away a layer of soil and sand. Once the coin was reported in the local news, an amateur historian called Peter Swift got in touch. He thought a settlement had stood here long before the castle was constructed. Then, quite unexpectedly, our team came across maps and papers in the library.

[02:15] AUDIO: They included drawings made five centuries ago of ruined buildings on the grass between the river and the castle's outer walls. At that point, we knew the theory was right. During our three seasons on the site, we've uncovered the remains of several buildings and an enormous quantity of broken, everyday pottery. What still hasn't appeared is a brooch or any other piece of jewelry.

[02:45] AUDIO: We have, however, found tools shaped from animal bone, and you'll be able to see those in the exhibition. There are also signs of activity on the bank opposite the castle. We haven't located any houses or small huts there, but the boundaries of an old system of fields can be traced. We initially took one long section of wall to be part of a palace.

[03:10] AUDIO: Further investigation showed that it was actually modern. This season's excavation is nearly over, though the team will return next summer. Before then, we're arranging guided visits for school groups in the autumn. You may already have watched the television documentary about us.

[03:30] AUDIO: It claimed our finds would go to the town museum, but that hasn't been decided. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. As you walk around, please remain on the marked paths.

[04:28] AUDIO: Let me point out several of the site's main features. Your current position is shown at the bottom of the map. This year we have established where an ancient bridge once stood. Divers are in the river today, looking for objects that may have been lost there.

[04:47] AUDIO: To reach its foundations, follow the main path straight ahead until it curves left. At that bend, take the narrower track on your right. It leads directly to the river and the diving team. Another feature worth seeing is the refuse pit, close against the castle walls at the northwest corner.

[05:12] AUDIO: It belongs to the castle period rather than the earlier village. The oyster shells and fish bones inside were probably discarded from the castle kitchen above. In our first summer, we located a communal hall. Two parallel lines of deep postholes told us that it had supported a substantial roof.

[05:38] AUDIO: It's the biggest building in the central part of the site, immediately beside the area we're excavating now. We found the village's fish pond last year. Such ponds were generally placed close to a river, whereas this one is some distance away, perhaps because the river's course has shifted. From here, turn right when you reach the first information board, then stay on the path into the trees.

[06:08] AUDIO: The pond is on your right before the path leaves the wooded area. If you arrive at the river, you've passed it. So, are there any...? That is the end of part two. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part two.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear Maya and Finn, two theater studies students, discussing their project on theater programs. First you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:50] MAYA: So Finn, I think I've taken my part of the research as far as I can. How are you getting on?

[00:57] FINN: Not too badly. I didn't realize Americans use the word playbill for a theater program. Until I began reading about the subject. It wasn't easy to find many worthwhile websites, but I'm still pleased we chose it.
[01:11] FINN: Nobody else on the course is covering the same topic, although it is one of our module leaders research interests.
[01:18] MAYA: That connection may actually have discouraged some people.
[01:22] FINN: Possibly. Another thing I hadn't known was that there are entire businesses devoted to producing theater programs.

[01:29] MAYA: They're fairly widespread these days. People often assume a theater pays a company to make its programs, but that's not how the arrangement works. The companies purchase the right to publish on a theater's behalf and then earn their income by selling space to advertisers inside the booklet.
[01:48] FINN: I can see why theaters find that more convenient.
[01:52] MAYA: Exactly.
[01:53] FINN: I came across some material about programs in the early days of British theater. The actors listed in them seemed to have mattered enormously.
[02:03] MAYA: Yes. Audiences knew the leading performers extremely well, and a celebrated name could bring in a huge crowd.

[02:13] FINN: What astonished me was that once a famous actor appeared on the program, the audience regarded it as a promise that the person would perform. If someone else went on instead, people claimed the theater had broken its agreement with them. They asked for their money back, and there were even riots when refunds were refused.
[02:35] MAYA: That's extraordinary. You couldn't imagine it happening now.
[02:40] FINN: No, even if the star misses a performance, disappointed audiences are much too restrained for that.

[02:47] MAYA: We should certainly put that point about early audiences in the project. We also need to explain that many ordinary people couldn't read then, so printed programs weren't much use for publicizing a play. When a troupe reached a town, the actors would advertise the performance themselves by marching through the streets in costume, beating drums, and calling out what they were going to stage.
[03:12] FINN: Interesting. That's another practice that's hard to picture today.
[03:16] MAYA: There's a useful contrast to draw between programs from the 18th and 19th centuries too.
[03:22] FINN: Didn't 19th century versions begin to look more like the programs we're familiar with now?
[03:28] MAYA: They did. Unlike those from the 18th century, they consistently included color.
[03:34] FINN: And their designs were more varied. Even so, I prefer the 18th century ones, because they gave the audience so much information, including details about the performers.
[03:47] MAYA: They covered the playwright and the story as well, and sometimes even included the play's background.
[03:54] FINN: That's right. What are we going to say about programs in the 20th century?
[03:59] MAYA: I think the major point is how sharply they changed during the Second World War.
[04:04] FINN: Because the government limited the amount of paper people could use.
[04:08] MAYA: Yes, though that only applied in Britain. American playbills kept the same format throughout.
[04:16] FINN: Here, however, a program was reduced to one sheet, folded into four pages of text.

[04:23] MAYA: What puzzles me is why, once the war ended, British programs stayed exactly like that for more than 25 years instead of expanding or changing. Paper remained scarce for perhaps another five or ten years, but not for the whole of that period.
[04:40] FINN: It is difficult to explain.
[04:43] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[05:29] MAYA: I've collected some images of programs that we could use on the slides for our presentation.
[05:34] FINN: I've found two as well. Let's work through them and decide which ones are useful.
[05:40] MAYA: All right, here's an old program for re-bloss.
[05:44] FINN: I don't know the play, but the program itself is very ornate.
[05:48] MAYA: You could frame it and hang it on a wall. The illustrations are beautiful. What have you got, Finn?

[05:55] FINN: Several pages from a program for Man of La Mancha. It's worth showing, not for its pictures, but for the articles contributed by people in the theater company. They reveal how the production was put together and what the cast thought and felt about it.

[06:12] MAYA: That would be useful. I also have a program that's now kept in a museum. It's for the tragedy of Jane Shore. It's believed to be the oldest surviving item printed on the first press ever used in Australia.
[06:27] FINN: That's remarkable.

[06:29] MAYA: We could also mention the program for the Sailors Festival. It's part of the British Library's digitized program collection, which was launched only a few years ago. The collection already contains more than 200,000 programs, which is incredible.
[06:46] FINN: I wish I'd discovered it while I was doing my research.
[06:52] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: Inclusive design
content: 📌 Inclusive design
Definition

Products are intended for people from a wide range of backgrounds and do not require any [ _____ ] to their original form.Universal design goes further by also considering users with [ _____ ] difficulties.
Examples of inclusive design

Adjustable [ _____ ] can reduce the risk of discomfort in the back or neck.Sensor-operated [ _____ ] in public toilets demand less hand movement.Design features for older users:interface designers tend not to use [ _____ ].commands may be given with a mouse, keyboard or [ _____ ].
Effects of non-inclusive design

AccessDisabled people may lose their independence.SafetySeatbelts create the greatest concern for [ _____ ] women.PPE jackets may fit badly because women's [ _____ ] can be considerably smaller than men's.The most serious PPE problems affect female [ _____ ] officers working in emergency services.Comfort at workThe [ _____ ] maintained in offices is frequently below a comfortable level for women.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a design and technology lecturer giving a talk about inclusive design. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Designers have only begun to give serious attention to inclusive products in fairly recent years.

[00:56] AUDIO: So, what exactly is meant by inclusive design? In simple terms, it involves creating products that cross financial, social and cultural boundaries. The aim is to make the original product usable by the widest possible variety of people without any adaptation being necessary. Inclusive design is frequently associated with universal design, though the two concepts are not identical.

[01:26] AUDIO: Universal design seeks to develop products that work for everybody. This means taking account of people with cognitive difficulties as well, which can be particularly demanding for designers. We can now see effective inclusive design in many ordinary settings. In offices, for instance, adjustable desks are increasingly common.

[01:51] AUDIO: They can be raised or lowered for users of different heights and for people in wheelchairs. Where suitable desks are not provided, workers may develop pain in the back or neck. Another familiar example appears in the public toilets of hotels, airports and office buildings. Sensor-operated taps do not have to be pushed or turned.

[02:18] AUDIO: As well as improving hygiene, they are much easier for anyone whose dexterity or mobility is limited. Technology companies were once criticized for concentrating too heavily on younger customers, but their approach is changing. A growing number of products are being created with older users in mind. Eye sight generally becomes poorer with age, and similar colours grow harder to tell apart.

[02:47] AUDIO: Blue shades are especially difficult, so software designers normally avoid blue when developing interfaces for elderly users. Ageing also affects motor control. Some people begin to struggle with simple actions, such as lifting a cup or opening a door, and using a mouse or keyboard may become difficult too. For this reason, voice access is now a standard alternative for giving commands.

[03:19] AUDIO: It is useful to consider what happens when designers fail to include a broad range of users, because the consequences can be serious. Access is an obvious concern, particularly because it affects the independence of disabled people. If buses and trains cannot accommodate wheelchairs, many people are unable to travel unless somebody accompanies them. Safety presents another problem.

[03:48] AUDIO: Surprisingly, the dummies used in most vehicle crash tests are still modelled on an average-sized man. This creates risks for women generally, but pregnant women are especially affected because the seat belts on those dummies have not been adapted for pregnancy. British workplaces have become much safer overall during the last century. Employers must provide any necessary personal protective equipment, or PPE, at no cost, and they are legally responsible for keeping it in good condition.

[04:26] AUDIO: This may include anything from protective glasses to a complete bodysuit. However, most PPE is still made to fit male bodies. One recent report found that employers sometimes assume a jacket designed for a small man will also suit a woman. Yet, a woman may be tall while having much narrower shoulders than the average man.

[04:51] AUDIO: Poorly fitting high-visibility jackets, vests and body armour can therefore place female workers in danger. In the same report, 95% of women said their PPE regularly interfered with their work. The problem was most severe in the emergency services, particularly among police officers. Workplace comfort creates a further difficulty.

[05:18] AUDIO: In summer, it is common to find women in offices wearing sweaters or wrapping themselves in blankets, while the air conditioning is running at full power. At the same time, male colleagues may be comfortable in shorts and t-shirts. The explanation lies in differences between male and female metabolic rates. Air conditioning is commonly set to a temperature of 21 degrees.

[05:47] AUDIO: A standard developed around men's needs. In many newer offices, staff cannot adjust that setting. Consequently, the temperature is often too low for women. Offices with mainly female staff may also waste energy because the air conditioning is kept at an unnecessarily high level.
[06:08] AUDIO: These examples show that failing to consider all potential users can have substantial consequences.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will now hear a man asking a friend for suggestions about what to do in the city with relatives who are bringing their children. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:50] MAN: Sandra, didn't you have some relatives staying with you not long ago?
[00:55] SANDRA: Yes, I did. My brother came with his family a couple of months back.
[01:00] MAN: Great. I was hoping you could give me a bit of advice. My cousin and her family are coming next month. And since I haven't got children myself, I'm not sure where I should take them.
[01:13] SANDRA: Right. Have they sorted out somewhere to stay? Will they be staying at your flat?
[01:18] MAN: No. Luckily, there simply isn't enough space. My cousin has asked me to suggest a hotel. Can you think of one?
[01:27] SANDRA: Actually, yes. I normally tell visitors to book the King's Hotel.
[01:32] MAN: What part of town is it in?
[01:34] SANDRA: It's only about a five-minute walk from Murray Station, so the location is very central. The hotel itself is on George Street.
[01:42] MAN: Oh, I know the place. They can't spend too much, though. Roughly what would a room cost?
[01:48] SANDRA: A family room is approximately 125 pounds a night, if you reserve one. My brother eventually chose two double rooms instead, and each of those came to about 95 pounds.
[02:04] MAN: That sounds fairly reasonable.
[02:06] SANDRA: How old are your cousin's children?
[02:09] MAN: They're 12 and 9. I'd like to arrange a few outings while they're here. As they've never visited the city, I thought a bus tour around the center might be a good start.

[02:20] SANDRA: The bus tours cost quite a lot. A walking tour would be a better choice, in my opinion. You get a much stronger sense of the city that way. There's one which leaves from Colton Square.
[02:32] SANDRA: It lasts around two hours and is reasonably priced.
[02:36] MAN: That sounds ideal. I'll find out more about it. Thanks.
[02:41] SANDRA: If you get good weather, you could take them to the old fort. There's a boat that goes there. The return trip takes about half a day altogether.
[02:50] MAN: That's a brilliant suggestion. I'd enjoy that trip as well. For a rainy day, I was considering the Science Museum. Perhaps they could visit while I'm working.
[03:02] SANDRA: Yes, but remember that the museum doesn't open on Mondays.
[03:06] MAN: They arrive on Saturday and are staying for four nights. So Tuesday seems the best day.
[03:12] SANDRA: It should be quieter then, too. Saturdays are incredibly busy. I took my children to the old computers exhibition there, and the crowds were awful. I meant to see it again.
[03:24] SANDRA: But that exhibition has ended now.
[03:26] MAN: That's unfortunate. My cousin's children would have liked it.
[03:31] SANDRA: A new exhibition about space is due to open soon, and that looks excellent as well.
[03:37] MAN: All right. I'll tell my cousin about it.
[03:42] NARRATOR: Before the conversation continues, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten. Now listen to the rest of the conversation and answer questions seven to ten.
[04:26] SANDRA: Have you decided where you might take everyone for meals?
[04:30] MAN: I'm a big fan of the food stalls in Clackton Market. My cousin is vegetarian. That market is one of the best places for vegetarian food.
[04:39] SANDRA: Absolutely. There'll be plenty for the children to choose from as well. You do have to arrive fairly early, though. At weekends, most stalls finish serving lunch at two thirty.
[04:51] MAN: Good point. I'll have to plan the timing carefully. My cousin also wants to take the children to a theater show, but the tickets are very costly.
[05:02] SANDRA: They are. However, if you use bargaintickets.com to book seats online for the next day, you can find some excellent offers. Certain seats are discounted by seventy-five percent.
[05:15] MAN: Really? I'll definitely see if I can get some.
[05:19] SANDRA: Good idea. And there are plenty of activities that won't cost anything. You don't need to spend a huge amount.
[05:27] MAN: What would you suggest?
[05:29] SANDRA: They're visiting next month, aren't they? Check whether their visit falls on the same weekend as the Roots Music Festival in Blakewell Gardens.
[05:38] MAN: Is that spelled R-O-O-T-S?
[05:41] SANDRA: Yes. You can look up the details online. It's always suitable for families, and admission is free.
[05:49] MAN: That would be perfect.

passages.title: The football stadium
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "The football stadium"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a guide speaking to members of the public during a visit to a football stadium in the UK. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to City Football Club.

[00:53] AUDIO: Before we begin the tour, I'll explain a few things about today's visit and the parts of the stadium you'll be able to see. There are quite a few children in the group, so I'd like parents to bear a couple of points in mind. We have a lot of steps here, and the tunnel used by the players is poorly lit. Please keep your children with you throughout the visit and don't allow them to go off alone, even briefly.

[01:19] AUDIO: That will help us avoid accidents and stop anyone becoming frightened. You're welcome to use cameras anywhere in the stadium. Later, your child can try taking a penalty and you'll be able to photograph them doing it. Our assistants will manage that activity, so with luck you won't be waiting in line for too long.

[01:40] AUDIO: The weather is very hot and bright on the pitch today. Food and cold drinks are available from the cafe, where I'd particularly recommend the nutritious lunch boxes made for children. While you're in the cafe, children can also enter today's football drawing competition. We'll choose the winning picture late this afternoon.

[02:01] AUDIO: Please write your name and contact information on the back, because if you've already gone home, we can post the prize to you. I'm afraid we aren't able to send the drawings back. Let me now describe some of the tour itself. We'll begin with the 360-degree cinema which visitors have enjoyed for several years.

[02:23] AUDIO: After that, I'll show you the players' changing rooms, and then we'll continue outside to the stands and the pitch. If you'd rather explore independently, you can now borrow headphones at reception and follow recorded commentary at your own pace. That audio service was launched this year, and we'd be grateful to hear what you think of it. We may provide tours in additional languages at some point, so comments on that idea would also be useful, and if you come back in the future, you could reserve one of our VIP tours online.

[02:58] AUDIO: Those tours are another service we've introduced this year. Before you hear the remainder of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15-20. Now listen and answer questions 15-20. The stadium standing here now dates from 1989 and was completed during a redevelopment program lasting three years.

[03:56] AUDIO: While the work was underway, the team played its home fixtures at another club's ground. With that one exception, this club has occupied the same site since 1870. That year marked the beginning of a particularly important period for football in Britain. It was in 1870 that teams first included a player specifically responsible for protecting the goal.

[04:21] AUDIO: It's difficult now to picture a match without someone performing that role. A number of new clubs appeared in 1872 and 1873, not only in this country but overseas as well. Then in 1874, referees gained the authority to dismiss players for particular offenses. A second rule introduced in the same year required the two teams to change ends at halftime.

[04:49] AUDIO: In the earliest games, a goal was scored by sending the ball between two flags. Later, the flags gave way to upright posts with tape stretched across the top. The familiar solid crossbar replaced that tape in 1875. More clubs were founded in 1877 and that was also when they collectively agreed that a match would last no more than 90 minutes.

[05:15] AUDIO: Previously, the finishing time had been informal. This sometimes led to serious disputes or even fights when one team wanted to stop but the other hoped to continue and score a winner. The football league contained more teams by 1878. Referees also began using whistles that year and electric lighting was fitted at some grounds.

[05:40] AUDIO: As a result, matches could take place in the evening and every season. In 1880, clubs started asking supporters to pay to enter matches. The players, however, were still amateurs with ordinary jobs, so they weren't receiving wages for playing. That contrasts sharply with today's professional game in which leading players earn large amounts both on the field and through commercial work.
[06:09] AUDIO: That is the end of part two. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Teaching handwriting
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Teaching handwriting"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two education students discussing an assignment about teaching children to write by hand. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:56] MAN: How are you progressing with the handwriting assignment?

[00:58] WOMAN: Fairly well. I hadn't appreciated how many different advantages children gain from learning to write. It's clearly a fundamental skill, although many people now regard it as less relevant because so little everyday writing is done by hand.
[01:17] MAN: Yes, and the research strongly supports teaching handwriting before keyboard skills. One reason is that forming letters manually strengthens children's recall.
[01:27] WOMAN: Exactly. The movement involved helps the shapes of letters remain in their minds. Once you consider it, that connection is quite easy to understand.
[01:41] MAN: What I didn't expect was the effect on children's ability to concentrate. Writing requires them to stay seated and direct their attention to a single task.
[01:51] WOMAN: I'd never thought of handwriting in that way either.
[01:53] MAN: Nor had I. I'm still less certain about why it encourages imagination.

[02:02] WOMAN: Remember the study of primary pupils? They produced a larger number of ideas when writing by hand than when working at a keyboard. That result was more or less what I would have predicted.
[02:15] MAN: Yes, me too. The link with awareness of space was another surprise for me. I'd always associated that ability with judging where your body is in relation to people or objects.

[02:28] WOMAN: So had I. But writers need a good sense of space to judge the gaps between words and place them correctly on a page. I'd assumed handwriting mainly developed precise hand movements, but its effects are much broader.

[02:44] MAN: Of course, handwriting presents much greater difficulties for children with dyspraxia because coordinating movement is hard for them. Fortunately, teachers can use several classroom activities to support them. Letter formation often needs a great deal of work. Games can help children tell similar letter forms apart, but progress in that area requires considerable patience.

[03:09] WOMAN: Yes. I liked the suggestion of giving them a special pen which produces a light when they push down with too much force. That provides immediate feedback and seems very straightforward.
[03:24] MAN: I agree completely. There isn't an equally direct way to deal with very slow writing. Accuracy should come first, and speed may increase later as confidence grows.
[03:34] WOMAN: Squared paper offers another simple form of support. If children put one letter in each square, they gradually learn to leave more consistent gaps.
[03:47] MAN: That's true. Improving the spacing has a greater effect on readability than making every word follow a perfectly straight line.
[03:58] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[04:41] MAN: For certain pupils, including some with dyslexia, learning on a laptop may work better than writing by hand. Handwriting can be so demanding for them that some stop trying.

[04:53] WOMAN: Yes. A wrong answer doesn't feel like such a serious setback on a computer, so they're generally more prepared to attempt the task again. However, the evidence says they don't achieve fluency any sooner.
[05:08] MAN: That's what I found as well. Did you see the article comparing print, where letters are separate, with cursive script, where they're connected?

[05:18] WOMAN: I did. Joined writing used to be viewed as more elegant and a sign of education, but that attitude has changed. Teachers now recognise that it takes longer to master, and connecting letters is especially demanding for pupils with learning difficulties.

[05:39] MAN: I agree. At school, I used to wonder whether my untidy writing lowered my examination results. Current research suggests that concern was justified. Many candidates probably feel they should be assessed only on what they know, rather than on the appearance of their work.

[05:59] WOMAN: Even so, assessors can't award credit for an answer they're unable to read, and studies show that marks can suffer. That's why readable handwriting has always been an important classroom goal. Do you expect handwriting to have a different role in the future?

[06:18] MAN: I doubt it will change greatly. It's unfortunate that most schools still don't teach touch typing. Perhaps that will matter less once people can write directly onto digital screens. In any case, teachers know handwriting remains a basic skill, so children will continue learning it.
[06:38] WOMAN: I think so too. Still, people depend increasingly on electronic devices and use pen and paper less often. That can weaken certain abilities.
[06:50] MAN: Do you mean taking notes? There are plenty of digital tools for recording those.

[06:56] WOMAN: Some people also mention difficulties with reading historical documents. My own problem is more immediate. My mother is amazed by my poor spelling and the irregular way I use punctuation. I'm sure that comes from not practising enough.

[07:14] MAN: Probably. I actually miss the habit of writing by hand. These days I hardly do it at all. My grandparents' writing was beautiful and distinctive, whereas nobody could recognise a note as mine now.
[07:28] MAN: I think we've lost something valuable.

[07:31] WOMAN: I feel the same. I once kept a handwritten diary, but now I type every entry because it takes less effort. Digital writing is convenient, but I'm sorry that handwriting has disappeared from so much of my daily life.

passages.title: Research in the area around the Cheme Bird Sanctuary
content: 📌 Research near the Kalewa Bat Reserve
The importance of bats to local communities

They destroy [ _____ ] and other crop pests.They help prevent farm workers from being bitten by [ _____ ].They have been an important part of the local culture for many years.They now support the economy by attracting [ _____ ] to the area.
Falling numbers of bats

The bats may be accidentally killed by [ _____ ] when feeding or migrating by electrocution from contact with power lines, especially during [ _____ ].Local fruit growers may illegally trap them or [ _____ ] them.
Ways of protecting fruit from bats

removing wild fruit trees from the area (unhelpful)placing a [ _____ ] around each orchard tree (expensive)frightening bats by keeping a [ _____ ] playing shining a [ _____ ], e.g. with battery lampsA [ _____ ] of methods is usually most effective.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 4. You will hear part of an environmental science lecture about the relationship between fruit bats and a farming community in Africa. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

[00:52] AUDIO: We've been examining conflicts that develop when protected wildlife feeds beyond the boundary of a reserve. I'd like to illustrate this with research I recently helped to conduct in northern Malawi in villages surrounding the Kalewa bat reserve. The reserve contains a network of caves and woodland used by 12 species of bat. Most families in the nearby villages grow fruit and maize on a small scale.

[01:21] AUDIO: Although bats sometimes feed in their orchards, the animals also provide important ecological and social benefits. Insect eating species, for instance, consume huge numbers of moths. The larvae of these moths can cause serious damage to maize before it is harvested, so the bats perform a valuable form of pest control. Their feeding habits protect people as well as crops.

[01:49] AUDIO: Mosquitoes are common around irrigation channels and their bites can transmit disease. By eating these insects after sunset, bats reduce the risk of farm workers being bitten while they are outdoors. People in the area have long understood these benefits. Stories and carvings featuring bats have been part of local culture for generations well before the reserve was officially established.

[02:16] AUDIO: In more recent years, the evening spectacle of thousands of bats leaving the caves has attracted increasing numbers of visitors. Their spending on guides, food and accommodation now provides useful income for several villages. Despite their protected status, however, bat numbers have been falling. Some deaths are accidental.

[02:41] AUDIO: A small wind farm was built outside the reserve several years ago, and bats can be struck by turbines while they are feeding at night or moving between seasonal roosts. The blades are difficult for them to detect when they are traveling quickly. Power infrastructure presents another danger. Bats occasionally land on high-voltage lines and may touch two live components at once.

[03:07] AUDIO: Electrocution is most common during storms, when strong gusts make controlled flight difficult and wet fur conducts electricity more readily. Fruit growers can also threaten the animals. When a large proportion of a crop is damaged, some farmers set traps, even though this is prohibited. A few have also been known to poison bats by treating pieces of fruit with agricultural chemicals.

[03:36] AUDIO: This is illegal and may harm owls and other animals that later eat the dead bats. So what can farmers do to protect their fruit without injuring wildlife? One suggestion has been to remove wild fruit trees from the edge of an orchard because these trees appear to attract bats. Our observations showed that this is actually counterproductive.

[04:02] AUDIO: The wild trees provide an alternative food supply and without them the bats concentrate more heavily on cultivated fruit. A more reliable option is to place a net around each orchard tree. If it is fitted properly, bats cannot reach the fruit. However, suitable material is costly and the net must be checked frequently so that birds do not become caught in it.

[04:29] AUDIO: For most small farms, protecting every tree in this way would be too expensive. Nearly all the farmers therefore spent time trying to frighten bats away without harming them. Some had tried keeping a dog in the orchard, but this made little difference because the bats remained well above the ground. A radio was much more useful.

[04:52] AUDIO: Farmers left one playing beside the trees during the first few hours after sunset and the changing voices and music discouraged bats from settling. Light provided another temporary deterrent. During the weeks when the fruit was ripening, family members took turns to shine a light into the branches whenever bats approached. Simple battery lamps were sufficient, although the beam had to be moved regularly because the bats soon became accustomed to a light that stayed in one position.

[05:25] AUDIO: No single measure worked all night or in every orchard. The farmers who lost the least fruit used a combination of methods, for example, a radio on most evenings, moving lights when bat activity increased, and nets on the most valuable trees. Even then, some damage continued, so our next stage will examine a longer-term solution that benefits both the farmers and the reserve.
